id: E-d mechanism: the town's dead given to the seam pay the keel's upkeep in sense (rule 5), and that is what keeps the valley warm
resembles: Final Fantasy VII (the Lifestream: the spirit energy and memories of the dead flow back into the planet, and Mako, which powers Midgar, is processed Lifestream, i.e. the dead)
Fullmetal Alchemist (the Philosopher's Stone: human souls as the fuel that pays alchemy's toll)
why: The pre-read already filed the world-break premise under FFVII (an empire drawing on something living under the land). E-d now adds FFVII's best-known lore fact on top: the energy under the ground is the dead, carrying their memories. A reader who caught the first FFVII echo will catch this one, and the two together read as a complete FFVII inversion. The real turn is that the heroes knowingly adopt Shinra's method, but the plan doesn't name that turn or design for it, and its echo table never mentions FFVII. 'Dead people pay the magic's price' is also FMA's Stone. The cost (survivors lose their memory of the dead) is fresher than the mechanism.
fix: Keep the cost and change what the dead give: let them pay by the link (their names, rule 3) being spent, not their sense being burned as fuel under the land, so it is the remembering that pays rather than the bodies. Or own the FFVII inversion on purpose and give the Hall faction the Shinra objection as its argument.

id: E-d / B51 / B11: the dead laid on the capstone, the warm stone the player respawns at, which warms from them; the founding event named 'the Kindling'
resembles: Dark Souls (bonfires built on the bones of the Undead, the coiled sword in a heap of bones and ash, Undead Bone Shards found in bonfires; 'kindling' a bonfire by spending Humanity; you return from death to the bonfire)
Dark Souls III (the Ashen One, the Lords of Cinder whose bodies are what the flame is fed)
why: A respawn point that is literally fed by the dead, in an ash-covered dark-fantasy world whose founding catastrophe is 'the Kindling', is the Dark Souls bonfire. The plan's Dark Souls row defends only the First Flame/champion reading ('no champion is spent') and misses the bonfire, which is the closer one and the one players see every hour. B11's warmer stone makes the player's own respawn point a corpse-fed fire on day 12. The vocabulary cluster (Kindling, ash, the kept, Keepers, a warm stone you return to) makes it worse: each word alone is fine, but together they are Dark Souls' word list.
fix: Keep the vigil but take the dead off the respawn stone: they go to a seam crack elsewhere (the Warm's custom from B27), and the capstone stays just where you wake. Rename 'the Kindling' (the renaming branch can take it).

id: E-d cost: the town can no longer remember its dead; the chronicle keeps names nobody can put to anyone
resembles: Coco (the second death when no one remembers you)
Ishiguro, The Buried Giant (a forgetting that keeps the peace; the 'giant' is the buried dead of a massacre)
Le Guin, The Other Wind / The Farthest Shore (in the dry land the dead do not know their loved ones)
Pratchett, Going Postal (the GNU overhead keeps dead names in motion)
why: Each is one step away: Coco is about the dead fading, Earthsea's dead forget the living, Buried Giant's forgetting covers everything and gets lifted. The living, knowingly and permanently, losing exactly the faces of the dead while keeping their names, as a running price, is not a known work's ending as far as I recall. Buried Giant is the nearest: buried dead under the land plus a communal forgetting that buys survival. The plan's defence of it holds, but 'the dead of the four buried towns carried up out of the layers' leans toward the Buried Giant image and is worth watching.

id: B49 / §1 point 1: 'the expected ending is spent as backstory'; a previous you tried sharing and the pages show it failed
resembles: Planescape: Torment (earlier incarnations' plans and journals record their failed attempts; you build on and against them)
Madoka Magica episode 10 (the earlier loops shown failing; the source of the old E-a redistribution, too)
Outer Wilds (the Nomai's recorded failed attempt at the answer)
Returnal / Prey 2017 (a past self's recordings of what didn't work)
why: 'The obvious solution was already tried, and here is the record of it failing' is a known device in exactly the works the pre-read named for the player's situation (Torment, Returnal). As a convention it is fine, and turning B49 from blueprint to failure is a real improvement over the old beat. But the plan offers it as its first point of freshness, and it isn't one; it is the Torment move. It also comes from the same past-self-in-the-ruins well the pre-read flagged as the player's real situation.
fix: Drop point 1 from the freshness argument rather than change the beat. Let the record be partly someone else's (a town-3 survivor's hand, or the tally alone) so it is not only a past you once again leaving the key document.

id: B49 logic: thirty people sharing the hold all forgot everything; E-d needs a town of 60
why: B49 is meant to rule sharing out, but the only fact it shows is that thirty people were not enough, and the cellar tally at B12 makes that count salient. The player's town at B49 is past the 60 gate. A sharp reader concludes 'thirty was too few; we are bigger' and expects the old E-a to work, which is exactly the reading the pre-read's own proposed turn ('too few people') invited. The elimination fails by headcount, and E-d's own population gate (double town 3) reinforces the inference. Why would a shared cost make each person lose everything rather than a little? The plan never says; rule 5 suggests the opposite.
fix: Make the failure not about numbers: the links between the sharers (rule 3) cascaded, so when one let go it took everyone, the Breaking in miniature, which a bigger town would make worse. One mark in the record (the first tick crossed through, then all of them) is enough to plant it.

id: B11 plant: the dead stranger's body leaves the warm stone 'warmer than it has ever been', wood dries twice as fast
why: The plan claims nothing is inferable before B39 (day 59). But B11 shows the mechanism outright on day 12, with a measurable effect, and the world's rules already teach that nothing is made, only moved (rule 1), and that humans carry more sense than any animal (the Taking). B18 at day 22 and B27 at day 38 repeat it. A genre reader has 'the dead feed the warmth' by day 38 at the latest, about 40 days before B50, which is the solved-early fault the plan says it avoids. 'Nobody remarks on it' does not help: the log line that reports the warmer stone is the remark.
fix: Keep the vigil as custom only at B11, with no physical effect, or one that a body's own heat explains. Let the first unambiguous warming be later (B35's dead route or B39's costing).

id: B44: N6's daybook lies open at the struck costing page while he says he has no other way
resembles: the spotlit Chekhov's gun
why: The ending's answer is pointed at with a staged prop at the moment the question is posed. It also raises a question the plan never answers: N6 wrote or kept that costing, so either he is lying when he says there is no other way, or he has a reason to reject it (irregular supply, the cost to grief) that should be on the page. Without that reason the open daybook is the narrative nudging the player. The answer still arrives as a found document (from the enemy's ledger rather than a past self's blueprint), which is the convenience the pre-read flagged in B49, moved to B39.
fix: Let N6's reason be visible and wrong-but-sane (he struck the line himself because the dead were not his to spend), and drop the open-at-the-page staging; the player already read the line at B39.

id: B35 O-price: the Warm elder offers a choice, goods or the town's dead to the seam, from now on
resembles: Frostpunk (the early law card on what to do with the dead: cemetery or snow pit, and later the dead used for the town's benefit; exact law names unsure)
why: The plan defends Frostpunk only for the ending ('a mid-game efficiency law'), but B35 is now precisely that: a mid-game binary choice, in a town surviving round a heat source, about whether the dead are buried or put to use. The pre-read already found the town, its faith role and its factions reading as Frostpunk, so this adds to an existing pile.
fix: Don't stage it as a two-price menu. Let the Warm simply take the town's dead when one dies near them, by custom, and let the player stop it or not afterwards.

id: B34 turn: N9 recognises the knot and takes you for your own child
resembles: the immortal taken for (or posing as) their own descendant: Highlander, The Age of Adaline, Forever (TV), Tuck Everlasting (unsure of the exact scene in the last)
why: The pre-read proposed it, but 'you must be his son' said to someone who hasn't aged is itself a staple of immortal stories. The knot-first recognition is the good part and holds; the mistaken-for-your-own-child turn is another famous turn.
fix: Keep the knot and cut the identification: N9 ties the knot back on the snare, says nothing, and stays near you; B40's date does the sum for both of you.

id: B16: a town-3 survivor whose hands kept the snare knot when the rest was gone
resembles: The Bourne Identity (the body keeps skills the mind lost)
why: Procedural memory surviving amnesia is a known device, but it is used on a stranger who is never explained, and it pays forward to B34 and B49. It works as a clue.

id: B40: the selection field reads 'present, no dependants'; the tick beside 'offered self' is yours
resembles: The Hunger Games ('I volunteer')
BioShock (the inversion the plan intends)
why: A volunteer is common, but the dry registry phrasing and its being about availability, not temperament, turns BioShock's conditioning reveal into the opposite. It holds.

id: B25 forged charcoal seal / B28 keepers filing you / B39 find-then-silence
resembles: Brazil
Papers, Please (unsure it is a fair echo)
Horizon Zero Dawn (what B25 turns)
why: Each turns 'the old machine knows only you' into clerical routine, in the register the pre-read called the freshest. B25's charcoal copy working once is especially good.

id: B32: the player holds a seam shut and the logging post freezes; a worker dies
resembles: Frostpunk (heat diverted from districts, people freeze)
why: Player-caused cost is the right fix for the told beat. The Frostpunk echo is in the subject (cold, heat) rather than in the turn.

id: B47: every lamp dims and everyone loses the same warmth, recorded in the journal's figures
resembles: Harry Potter's dementors (cold)
why: A god implied by an even, measured debit in a ledger is the pre-read's suggested turn, and I know no work that does it.

id: B13 / B18 / B21 changes (the old don't look up; fungus walks an elk; 'never thank the warmth')
resembles: Bradbury, 'All Summer in a Day'
cordyceps in ants (nature; The Last of Us's origin)
fae etiquette (thanks admits a debt)
why: Each keeps a convention and changes the payoff. The elk is a nature image more than a TLoU image once no human walks. The fae echo in the taboo is real, but it makes the debt literal.

id: B52 / B53 / B16: N9 can't call up her mother's face 'and still ties the knot'; a man sets out a second cup; roofs swept anyway out of habit
resembles: the empty place set for the dead (stock grief image)
why: Three closing images in a row now say the same thing: the habit outlives the loss (the knot, the cup, the sweeping), and B16 said it earlier. The repeated shape is the sameness tell, and 'and still ties the knot' is a consoling grace note added straight after the bite, which softens the dark register the pre-read asked B52 to keep. The second cup for someone you can't name is the stock image of grief.
fix: End N9's line on the face she can't call up, with no consoling clause. Replace the second cup with an object only this world has (a name in the chronicle someone reads aloud and can't place), and leave the habit image to B53 alone.

id: §1 'Why a genre reader hasn't seen it end this way' and the echo tables
why: The defence is written in the register of a pitch: five numbered points of freshness, each 'differs' row closed with a reason. Two of the five don't hold (point 1 is Torment's device; point 3, grief as the price, is the Buried Giant's ground), and the table omits the two closest works (FFVII's Lifestream and Dark Souls' bonfire). 'It is irregular, as the Concord said' is a neat bow: the clerk's reason for rejecting the line becomes the ending's risk. That irony is fine in the story but it is the tidy kind; let it stay unremarked in player text.
fix: Replace the freshness argument with the honest list of nearest works and what each shares, and let the human cold read decide.
